questions.q: The following plots show variation of velocity ($v$) with time ($t$), of a ball thrown vertically upward, and falling back. Which of the following plots is/are correct ?
questions.solution:
Let the upward direction be considered positive.

When a ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity $u$, it moves under the constant downward acceleration due to gravity ($a = -g$).

The velocity $v$ at any time $t$ is given by the kinematic equation:
$v = u + at$
$\Rightarrow v = u - gt$

This equation represents a straight line with a positive y-intercept ($u$) and a constant negative slope ($-g$).

Initially, the velocity is positive and decreases linearly until it becomes zero at the highest point. As the ball falls back down, the velocity becomes negative and its magnitude increases linearly.

Plot C correctly shows a straight line starting from a positive value on the v-axis, crossing the t-axis, and continuing with a constant negative slope.

Answer: C only

questions.q: Consider a particle moving along a straight line, whose position as a function of time is given by $s(t)=\alpha t^2-\beta t+\gamma$, where $\alpha=1$ ms$^{-2}$, $\beta=6$ ms$^{-1}$ and $\gamma=5$ m. The average speed of the particle, in ms$^{-1}$, from $t=0$ to $t=6$ s is :
questions.solution:
Given $s(t) = t^2 - 6t + 5$

Velocity $v(t) = \dfrac{ds}{dt} = 2t - 6$

The particle comes to rest when $v(t) = 0$, which gives $t = 3$ s.

Position at $t = 0$ s is $s(0) = 5$ m.

Position at $t = 3$ s is $s(3) = 3^2 - 6(3) + 5 = -4$ m.

Position at $t = 6$ s is $s(6) = 6^2 - 6(6) + 5 = 5$ m.

Distance travelled from $t = 0$ to $t = 3$ s is $d_1 = |-4 - 5| = 9$ m.

Distance travelled from $t = 3$ to $t = 6$ s is $d_2 = |5 - (-4)| = 9$ m.

Total distance travelled is $D = d_1 + d_2 = 9 + 9 = 18$ m.

Average speed $= \dfrac{18}{6} = 3$ ms$^{-1}$

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
When a ruler falls vertically, $5$ different persons catch it with different reaction times. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$)
A. Person A has reaction time of $0.20$ s.
B. Person B has reaction time of $0.22$ s.
C. Person C has reaction time of $0.18$ s.
D. Person D has reaction time of $0.19$ s.
E. Person E has reaction time of $0.21$ s.
What is the correct order of the distance travelled by the ruler for each person ?
questions.solution:
The distance travelled by the ruler falling freely under gravity is given by $d = \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2$.

Since $g$ is constant, the distance $d$ is directly proportional to the square of the reaction time $t$. Thus, a larger reaction time results in a greater distance travelled by the ruler.

The given reaction times are:
$t_A = 0.20$ s
$t_B = 0.22$ s
$t_C = 0.18$ s
$t_D = 0.19$ s
$t_E = 0.21$ s

Arranging the reaction times in descending order:
$0.22 \gt 0.21 \gt 0.20 \gt 0.19 \gt 0.18$

This corresponds to:
$t_B \gt t_E \gt t_A \gt t_D \gt t_C$

Therefore, the correct order of the distance travelled by the ruler is:
$B \gt E \gt A \gt D \gt C$

Answer: $B \gt E \gt A \gt D \gt C$

Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct

Both statement I and statement II are incorrect
questions.solution:
The work done in stopping the car and the truck can be written as
W=Fx=∆KE
As both the car and the truck are moving initially with the same kinetic energy, after being stopped, they will have the same change of kinetic energy.
Also, they are stopped with the same applied force.
Hence, from the above equation, it can be written that they have the same displacement, i.e., x1=x2.
Acceleration is a vector quantity. As the direction of motion of the car is different in the two given situations, the acceleration of the car will not be the same.

Also, an object can have varying velocity without varying speed (e.g., constant speed with changing direction). The assertion states the opposite.
- Reason is true: When a ball is thrown upwards, its velocity is instantaneously zero at the peak of its trajectory, but the acceleration due to gravity is still acting downwards (\(\mathrm{g} \neq 0)\).

questions.q:
Assertion : On a curved path, average speed of a particle can never be equal to average velocity.
Reason : Average speed is total distance travelled divided by total time. Whereas average velocity is final velocity, plus initial velocity divided by two.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Assertion is true: On a curved path, the displacement (a straight line from start to end) is always less than the distance traveled along the curve. Since average velocity = displacement/time and average speed = distance/time, and time is the same, average speed will be greater than average velocity (unless the path is straight and there's no change in direction, which is not the case for a curved path).
Reason is false: Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time, not (final velocity + initial velocity) / 2. The latter is true only for uniformly accelerated motion.

Reason : If the direction of change in velocity vector changes, the direction of acceleration vector also Changes.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Assertion is false: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If the direction of velocity remains unchanged, it means the motion is along a straight line without any change in direction. In such a case, for acceleration to change direction, the velocity would also have to change its direction, which contradicts the assertion. For example, in projectile motion, acceleration (due to gravity) is constant downwards, but the velocity vector continuously changes direction.
Reason is true: Acceleration is defined as \(\Delta \mathrm{v} / \Delta \mathrm{t}\). If the direction of the change in velocity vector (\(\Delta \mathrm{v}\)) changes, then the direction of the acceleration vector (a) also changes.

Reason is correct: The concavity of the position-time graph gives information about the sign of acceleration. A concave up curve indicates positive acceleration, and a concave down curve indicates negative acceleration.
The reason provides a correct statement about position-time graphs and acceleration, but it doesn't fully explain how plotting an acceleration-time graph is possible from a position-time graph (which involves two steps: position to velocity, then velocity to acceleration).

options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Assertion is correct: A v-t graph perpendicular to the time axis means that for a single instant of time, there are infinite values of velocity, which is physically impossible. This implies an instantaneous, infinite change in velocity.
Reason is correct: Infinite acceleration means an instantaneous change in velocity. Since acceleration \(=\Delta \mathrm{v} / \Delta \mathrm{t}\), if \(\Delta \mathrm{t}\) approaches zero (as in a vertical line on a v-t graph), and \(\Delta \mathrm{v}\) is finite, then acceleration approaches infinity, which cannot be realized in practice. The reason correctly explains why the assertion is true.

If both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Assertion is correct: If velocity is constant, it means both its magnitude (speed) and direction are constant. In this case, the distance traveled is equal to the magnitude of the displacement, and thus, average speed (total distance/total time) will be equal to the magnitude of average velocity (magnitude of total displacement/total time).
Reason is correct: Constant velocity implies that the object is moving in a straight line without changing its direction. This is why the distance equals the magnitude of the displacement. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

If both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Assertion is true: Let velocity of \(A\) be \(\mathrm{v} \_A=v \mathrm{i}\) (eastwards) and velocity of \(B\) be \(\mathrm{v} \_B=v \mathrm{j}\) (northwards), where \(v\) is the speed. The velocity of \(A\) with respect to \(B\) is \(\mathrm{v} \_A B=\mathrm{v} \_A-\mathrm{v} \_B=v \mathrm{i}\) -vj . This vector has a positive x -component and a negative y -component, which corresponds to the south-east direction.
Reason is false: Relative velocity is zero only if both the magnitude and direction of the velocities are the same. Here, only the magnitudes (speeds) are the same, but their directions are perpendicular (east vs. north). Therefore, their relative velocity is not zero.

Reason is correct: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If velocity is changing its direction or magnitude, even if it momentarily becomes zero, acceleration can still be non-zero as it represents the tendency to change velocity. The reason correctly explains the assertion by defining acceleration as the rate of change of velocity, meaning that a change is still occurring or imminent even if velocity is momentarily zero.

\hline
(A) & \frac{d \mathrm{v}}{dt} & (p) & \text{Acceleration} \\
\hline
(B) & \frac{d |\mathrm{v}|}{dt} & (q) & \text{Magnitude of acceleration} \\
\hline
(C) & \frac{d \mathrm{r}}{dt} & (r) & \text{Velocity} \\
\hline
(D) & \left|\frac{d \mathrm{r}}{dt}\right| & (s) & \text{Magnitude of velocity} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
- Part A: \(\frac{d y}{d t}\)
- This is the time derivative of velocity. By definition, the rate of change of velocity is acceleration. Since velocity is a vector, its derivative is also a vector, representing acceleration.
- Therefore, (A) matches with (p) Acceleration.
- Part B: \(\frac{d|v|}{d t}\)
- This is the time derivative of the magnitude of velocity (speed). This quantity is the rate of change of speed. This is NOT the same as the magnitude of acceleration. For example, in uniform circular motion, the speed is constant, so \(\frac{d|v|}{d t}=0\), but the object is accelerating because its direction is changing. The magnitude of acceleration is nonzero in this case.
- Therefore, (B) matches with (q) Magnitude of acceleration.
- Part C: \(\frac{d r}{d t}\)
- This is the time derivative of the position vector. By definition, the rate of change of position is velocity.
- Therefore, (C) matches with (r) Velocity.
- Part D: \(\frac{|d r|}{d t}\)
- The term \(\frac{|d r|}{d t}\) is the magnitude of the rate of change of the position vector. As we know, \(\frac{d r}{d t}\) is the velocity, so taking its magnitude gives us the magnitude of velocity or speed.
- Therefore, (D) matches with (s) Magnitude of velocity.

Let us cell a motion, \(A\) when velocity is positive and increasing \(A^{-1}\) when velocity is negative and increasing. \(R\) when velocity is positive and decreasing and \(R^{-1}\) when velocity is negative and decreasing. Now, match the following two columns for the given \(s-t\) graph.
\(\begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|} \hline & \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\ \hline (A) & M & (p) & A^{-1} \\ \hline (B) & N & (q) & R^{-1} \\ \hline (C) & P & (r) & A \\ \hline (D) & Q & (s) & R \\ \hline \end{array}\)
questions.solution:
Rule: velocity \(=\) slope of \(s-t\) curve (sign from slope), velocity increasing/decreasing \(=\) sign of acceleration = concavity of \(s(t)\) (concave up \(\rightarrow\) acceleration \(\gt 0 \rightarrow\) velocity increasing; concave down \(\rightarrow\) acceleration \(\lt 0 \rightarrow\) velocity decreasing).
Apply at marked points:
- \(M\) : slope negative, curve concave up \(\rightarrow\) velocity negative and increasing \(\rightarrow A^{-1}\).
- \(N\) : slope negative, curve concave down \(\rightarrow\) velocity negative and decreasing \(\rightarrow R^{-1}\).
- \(P\) : slope positive, curve concave up \(\rightarrow\) velocity positive and increasing \(\rightarrow A\).
- \(Q\) : slope positive, curve concave down \(\rightarrow\) velocity positive and decreasing \(\rightarrow R\).
So matching: \(M \rightarrow p\left(A^{-1}\right), N \rightarrow q\left(R^{-1}\right), P \rightarrow r(A), Q \rightarrow s(R)\). (Choice 1.)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A car starting from rest and moving with uniform acceleration covers 5 times the distance in the $3^{\text{rd}}$ second as it does in the $1^{\text{st}}$ second.

Reason (R): For a body starting from rest with uniform acceleration, the distance covered in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second is directly proportional to $n^2$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion (A): For a body starting from rest ($u = 0$) with uniform acceleration $a$, the distance covered in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second is given by $S_n = \dfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$.
For $n = 1$, $S_1 = \dfrac{a}{2}(1)$.
For $n = 3$, $S_3 = \dfrac{a}{2}(5) = 5 S_1$.
Thus, the car covers 5 times the distance in the $3^{\text{rd}}$ second as it does in the $1^{\text{st}}$ second. The Assertion is true.

Reason (R): The distance covered in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second is proportional to $(2n-1)$, which represents an arithmetic progression of odd numbers (Galileo's law of odd numbers). It is the total distance covered in $n$ seconds that is proportional to $n^2$. Therefore, the Reason is false.

Hence, (A) is true but (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A passenger sitting in a train compartment drops a small bolt from a height $h$ above the floor. Let $t_1$ be the time taken by the bolt to reach the floor when the train is moving straight along a horizontal track with a constant speed $v$. Let $t_2$ be the time taken when the train is completely stationary. Which of the following relationships is correct?
options: The relationship depends on the magnitude of $v$
questions.solution:
Since the train is moving with a constant speed $v$ along a straight horizontal track, its acceleration is zero.

The vertical motion of the bolt is independent of the horizontal uniform motion of the train. The initial vertical velocity of the bolt relative to the train is zero, and the relative vertical acceleration is $g$ downwards.

Using the second equation of motion for the relative vertical motion, $h = u_{rel}t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{rel}t^2$.

Since $u_{rel} = 0$ and $a_{rel} = g$, the time taken is $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

This time is independent of the train's constant horizontal velocity. Therefore, the time taken in the moving train is exactly the same as in the stationary train, so $t_1 = t_2$.

Answer: $t_1 = t_2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A boy walks from his home to a store along a straight path at a constant speed $v_1$. He returns to his home along the same path at an unknown constant speed $v_2$. If the average speed for his entire round trip is $V$, which of the following expressions correctly gives $v_2$?
questions.solution:
Let the distance from home to the store be $d$. The total distance for the round trip is $2d$.

Time taken for the outbound journey, $t_1 = \dfrac{d}{v_1}$.
Time taken for the return journey, $t_2 = \dfrac{d}{v_2}$.

Total time taken, $T = t_1 + t_2 = \dfrac{d}{v_1} + \dfrac{d}{v_2} = d \left( \dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{v_1 v_2} \right)$.

The average speed $V$ for the entire trip is given by total distance divided by total time:
$V = \dfrac{2d}{d \left( \dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{v_1 v_2} \right)} = \dfrac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$.

Rearranging the equation to solve for $v_2$:
$V(v_1 + v_2) = 2 v_1 v_2$
$V v_1 + V v_2 = 2 v_1 v_2$
$V v_1 = 2 v_1 v_2 - V v_2$
$V v_1 = v_2(2 v_1 - V)$
$v_2 = \dfrac{V v_1}{2 v_1 - V}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{V v_1}{2 v_1 - V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle moves along the positive $x$-axis. It travels from $x = 0$ to $x = L$ at a constant speed $v$, and then from $x = L$ to $x = 3L$ at a constant speed $3v$. The average speed of the particle for the entire journey is:
questions.solution:
Total distance travelled by the particle is $\Delta x = 3L - 0 = 3L$.

Time taken for the first part of the journey (from $x = 0$ to $x = L$) is:
$t_1 = \dfrac{L}{v}$

Time taken for the second part of the journey (from $x = L$ to $x = 3L$) is:
$t_2 = \dfrac{3L - L}{3v} = \dfrac{2L}{3v}$

Total time taken is:
$t = t_1 + t_2 = \dfrac{L}{v} + \dfrac{2L}{3v} = \dfrac{5L}{3v}$

Average speed is given by:
$v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Total time}} = \dfrac{3L}{\dfrac{5L}{3v}} = \dfrac{9v}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{9v}{5}$

questions.q: An elevator is accelerating vertically upwards at a rate of $\dfrac{g}{3}$. A person inside the elevator drops a ball from a height $h$ above the elevator floor. What is the time taken for the ball to reach the floor?
questions.solution:
Let the upward direction be positive and downward be negative.

Acceleration of the elevator, $a_{e} = +\dfrac{g}{3}$
Acceleration of the freely falling ball with respect to the ground, $a_{b} = -g$

The relative acceleration of the ball with respect to the elevator is:
$a_{\text{rel}} = a_{b} - a_{e} = -g - \left(+\dfrac{g}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{4g}{3}$
The magnitude of relative acceleration is $\dfrac{4g}{3}$ downwards.

The initial relative velocity of the ball is zero ($u_{\text{rel}} = 0$).
Using the second equation of motion for relative motion:
$s_{\text{rel}} = u_{\text{rel}}t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{\text{rel}}t^2$
$h = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{4g}{3}\right)t^2$
$h = \dfrac{2g}{3}t^2$
$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{3h}{2g}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{3h}{2g}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cyclist rides along a highway. A fleet of autonomous delivery pods leaves a depot in both directions every $15 \text{ minutes}$ at a constant speed of $60 \text{ km/h}$. The ratio of the time interval between pods overtaking the cyclist to the time interval between pods crossing the cyclist from the opposite direction is $3:1$. What is the cyclist's speed and the exact time interval between opposite-direction encounters?
questions.solution:
Let the speed of the cyclist be $v_c$. The speed of the pods is $v_p = 60 \text{ km/h}$.

The distance $d$ between consecutive pods in either direction is:
$d = v_p \times T = 60 \times \dfrac{15}{60} = 15 \text{ km}$

The time interval for pods overtaking the cyclist (same direction) is:
$t_{\text{overtake}} = \dfrac{d}{v_p - v_c}$

The time interval for pods crossing from the opposite direction is:
$t_{\text{opposite}} = \dfrac{d}{v_p + v_c}$

Given the ratio $t_{\text{overtake}} : t_{\text{opposite}} = 3 : 1$, we have:
$\dfrac{v_p + v_c}{v_p - v_c} = 3$
$60 + v_c = 3(60 - v_c)$
$60 + v_c = 180 - 3v_c$
$4v_c = 120 \Rightarrow v_c = 30 \text{ km/h}$

Now, calculate the time interval for opposite-direction encounters:
$t_{\text{opposite}} = \dfrac{d}{v_p + v_c} = \dfrac{15}{60 + 30} = \dfrac{15}{90} \text{ h}$
$t_{\text{opposite}} = \dfrac{1}{6} \text{ h} = 10 \text{ min}$

Answer: $30 \text{ km/h}, 10 \text{ min}$

questions.q: Two cars, X and Y, are in uniform motion. The ratio of the speed of car X to the speed of car Y is $1:3$. If the position-time graph of car X makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the time axis, what is the angle made by the position-time graph of car Y with the time axis?
questions.solution:
The slope of a position-time graph represents the velocity (or speed, for uniform motion in one direction) of the object.

Let $v_X$ and $v_Y$ be the speeds of cars X and Y respectively.
We know that $v = \tan(\theta)$, where $\theta$ is the angle made with the time axis.

For car X:
$v_X = \tan(30^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

Given the ratio of speeds:
$\dfrac{v_X}{v_Y} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Substituting $v_X$:
$\dfrac{1/\sqrt{3}}{v_Y} = \dfrac{1}{3}$
$\Rightarrow v_Y = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}$

For car Y:
$v_Y = \tan(\theta_Y) = \sqrt{3}$
$\Rightarrow \theta_Y = 60^\circ$

The angle made by the position-time graph of car Y with the time axis is $60^\circ$.

Answer: $60^\circ$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Freight trains, each of length $500 \text{ m}$, leave a station every $10 \text{ minutes}$ at a constant speed of $90 \text{ km/h}$. A car drives on a parallel road in the opposite direction at a constant speed of $60 \text{ km/h}$. What is the ratio of the time interval between the car meeting the front of successive trains to the time duration the car spends alongside a single train?
questions.solution:
The distance $d$ between the heads of successive trains depends only on the train's speed and the departure period.

$d = v_{\text{train}} \times T = 90 \text{ km/h} \times \left(\dfrac{10}{60}\right) \text{ h} = 15 \text{ km}$

The relative speed between the car and the trains is $v_{\text{rel}} = 90 + 60 = 150 \text{ km/h}$.

The time interval between the car meeting the front of successive trains is $t_1 = \dfrac{d}{v_{\text{rel}}}$.

The time duration the car spends alongside a single train of length $L = 500 \text{ m} = 0.5 \text{ km}$ is $t_2 = \dfrac{L}{v_{\text{rel}}}$.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{t_1}{t_2} = \dfrac{d / v_{\text{rel}}}{L / v_{\text{rel}}} = \dfrac{d}{L}$.

Ratio $= \dfrac{15 \text{ km}}{0.5 \text{ km}} = 30$.

Thus, the ratio is $30 : 1$.

Answer: $30 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles P and Q are moving along the x-axis. Their position-time graphs are straight lines making angles of $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ respectively with the time axis. If the axes are drawn in SI units, the magnitude of the relative velocity of P with respect to Q is:
questions.solution:
The velocity of a particle is given by the slope of its position-time graph, which is the tangent of the angle it makes with the time axis.

The velocity of particle P is:
$v_P = \tan(60^\circ) = \sqrt{3} \text{ m/s}$

The velocity of particle Q is:
$v_Q = \tan(30^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ m/s}$

Since both slopes are positive, the particles are moving in the same direction along the x-axis. The magnitude of the relative velocity of P with respect to Q is:
$v_{PQ} = |v_P - v_Q| = \sqrt{3} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$v_{PQ} = \dfrac{3 - 1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ m/s}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a particle travels between two points with speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$ ($v_1 \neq v_2$) for two equal time intervals, its average speed is strictly greater than if it travels with the same speeds for two equal distances.

Reason (R): The arithmetic mean of two distinct positive numbers is always greater than their harmonic mean.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
For a particle travelling with speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$ for two equal time intervals, the average speed is the arithmetic mean (AM):
$v_{avg, time} = \dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{2}$

For a particle travelling with the same speeds for two equal distances, the average speed is the harmonic mean (HM):
$v_{avg, dist} = \dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$

By the mathematical property of positive distinct numbers, the arithmetic mean is strictly greater than the harmonic mean (AM > HM).
Therefore, $v_{avg, time} \gt v_{avg, dist}$.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List I with List II for a freely falling body dropped from rest.

(A)Total distances fallen in 1 s, 2 s, 3 s(I)$1:3:5$
(B)Distances fallen in the $1^{\text{st}}$, $2^{\text{nd}}$, and $3^{\text{rd}}$ seconds(II)$1:2:3$
(C)Velocities at the end of 1 s, 2 s, 3 s(III)$1:(\sqrt{2}-1):(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})$
(D)Times taken to fall successive equal distances $h$(IV)$1:4:9$


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For a freely falling body dropped from rest, the initial velocity $u = 0$ and acceleration $a = g$.

(A) Total distance fallen in time $t$ is $S = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Thus, $S \propto t^2$. For $t = 1, 2, 3$ s, the ratio is $1^2 : 2^2 : 3^2 = 1:4:9$.

(B) Distance fallen specifically in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second is $S_n = \dfrac{g}{2}(2n-1)$. Thus, $S_n \propto (2n-1)$. For $n = 1, 2, 3$, the ratio is $1:3:5$.

(C) Velocity at time $t$ is $v = gt$. Thus, $v \propto t$. For $t = 1, 2, 3$ s, the ratio is $1:2:3$.

(D) Time taken to fall a distance $h$ from rest is $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$. The time to fall successive equal distances $h$ is the difference in total times: $t_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$, $t_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{4h}{g}} - \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$, $t_3 = \sqrt{\dfrac{6h}{g}} - \sqrt{\dfrac{4h}{g}}$. The ratio is $1 : (\sqrt{2}-1) : (\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})$.

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A train covers the first half of its total journey distance at a speed of $40 \text{ km/h}$. To achieve an overall average speed of $48 \text{ km/h}$ for the entire journey, what must be its speed for the second half of the distance?
questions.solution:
Let the total distance be $2d$. The train covers distance $d$ at $v_1 = 40 \text{ km/h}$ and the remaining distance $d$ at speed $v_2$.

For two equal distances covered at different speeds, the average speed $v_{\text{avg}}$ is given by the harmonic mean:
$v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$

Substitute the given values ($v_{\text{avg}} = 48 \text{ km/h}$ and $v_1 = 40 \text{ km/h}$):
$48 = \dfrac{2 \times 40 \times v_2}{40 + v_2}$

$48(40 + v_2) = 80 v_2$

$1920 + 48 v_2 = 80 v_2$

$32 v_2 = 1920$

$v_2 = \dfrac{1920}{32} = 60 \text{ km/h}$

Answer: $60 \text{ km/h}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is projected vertically upwards from the surface of the earth and returns to the same starting point. Taking the upward direction as positive and the starting point as the origin, which of the following correctly describes the position-time ($y-t$) graph for this motion?
options: Two straight line segments forming a triangle with its peak above the time axis.
An upward-opening parabolic curve starting from the origin.
A semi-circular arc starting from the origin and ending on the time axis.
A downward-opening parabolic curve starting from the origin and returning to the time axis.
questions.solution:
Let the initial velocity be $u$ (upwards, so positive). The acceleration due to gravity is $a = -g$ (downwards).

The position $y$ of the particle at any time $t$ is given by the second equation of motion:
$y = ut - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$

This is a quadratic equation in $t$. Since the coefficient of $t^2$ is negative ($-\dfrac{1}{2}g$), the graph of $y$ versus $t$ is a parabola opening downwards.

At $t = 0$, $y = 0$. The particle reaches a maximum positive height and then returns to $y = 0$. Therefore, the graph is a downward-opening parabolic curve starting from the origin and returning to the time axis.

A triangle would imply constant velocity, an upward-opening parabola would imply positive acceleration, and a semi-circle is a common misconception confusing the spatial trajectory of a 2D projectile with a 1D position-time graph.

Answer: A downward-opening parabolic curve starting from the origin and returning to the time axis.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car travelling on a straight highway covers one-third of its total journey distance at a speed of $10 \text{ km/h}$, and the remaining two-thirds of the distance at a speed of $60 \text{ km/h}$. The average speed of the car for the entire journey is
questions.solution:
Let the total distance of the journey be $3x$.

The distance covered in the first part is $x$ at a speed of $v_1 = 10 \text{ km/h}$.
Time taken for the first part, $t_1 = \dfrac{x}{10} \text{ h}$.

The distance covered in the second part is $2x$ at a speed of $v_2 = 60 \text{ km/h}$.
Time taken for the second part, $t_2 = \dfrac{2x}{60} = \dfrac{x}{30} \text{ h}$.

Total time taken, $T = t_1 + t_2 = \dfrac{x}{10} + \dfrac{x}{30} = \dfrac{3x + x}{30} = \dfrac{4x}{30} = \dfrac{2x}{15} \text{ h}$.

Average speed is defined as the ratio of total distance to total time:
$v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Total time}} = \dfrac{3x}{\dfrac{2x}{15}} = \dfrac{45}{2} = 22.5 \text{ km/h}$.

Answer: $22.5 \text{ km/h}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An observer moves at a constant speed $v_0$ parallel to a regular service of buses. The buses operate in both directions at a constant speed $v_b$ (where $v_b \gt v_0$) with a departure time period $T$. Consider the following statements:

A. The spatial distance between two consecutive buses moving in the same direction is $(v_b - v_0)T$.
B. The time interval between the observer's encounters with buses moving in the opposite direction is strictly less than $T$.
C. If the observer's speed $v_0$ increases, the time interval between encounters with buses moving in the same direction also increases.
D. The relative speed of buses moving in one direction with respect to buses moving in the opposite direction is zero.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement A is incorrect: The spatial distance between consecutive buses depends only on the bus speed and departure period, given by $d = v_b T$, which is independent of the observer's speed.

Statement B is correct: The time interval for opposite direction encounters is $t_{\text{opp}} = \dfrac{d}{v_b + v_0} = \dfrac{v_b T}{v_b + v_0}$. Since $v_b + v_0 \gt v_b$, it follows that $t_{\text{opp}} \lt T$.

Statement C is correct: The time interval for same direction encounters is $t_{\text{same}} = \dfrac{d}{v_b - v_0} = \dfrac{v_b T}{v_b - v_0}$. As $v_0$ increases, the denominator $(v_b - v_0)$ decreases, causing $t_{\text{same}}$ to increase.

Statement D is incorrect: The relative speed between buses moving in opposite directions is $v_b - (-v_b) = 2v_b$, not zero.

Therefore, exactly two statements (B and C) are correct.

Answer: Only two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements regarding the interpretation of position-time graphs for uniform motion:

Statement I: If the position-time graphs of two moving particles make angles of $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ with the time axis, the ratio of their velocities is $1:2$.
Statement II: The velocity of a particle in uniform motion is directly proportional to the angle its position-time graph makes with the time axis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
questions.solution:
The velocity of a particle is given by the slope of its position-time graph, which is equal to the tangent of the angle ($\theta$) the graph makes with the time axis, i.e., $v = \tan(\theta)$.

Statement I is incorrect because the ratio of velocities for angles $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ is:
$\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{\tan(30^\circ)}{\tan(60^\circ)} = \dfrac{1/\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$, not $1:2$.

Statement II is incorrect because velocity is directly proportional to the tangent of the angle ($\tan(\theta)$), not the angle ($\theta$) itself. For example, doubling the angle from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ increases the velocity by a factor of 3, not 2.

Therefore, both statements are incorrect.

Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stone is dropped from a tall tower. The distance it falls in the last second of its motion is exactly equal to the total distance it falls in the first $3$ seconds. What is the total height of the tower? (Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Let the total time of fall be $n$ seconds.

The total distance fallen in the first $3$ seconds is:
$S_3 = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (3)^2 = 5 \times 9 = 45 \text{ m}$

The distance fallen in the last ($n^{\text{th}}$) second is given by:
$S_n = u + \dfrac{g}{2}(2n - 1)$
Since the stone is dropped, $u = 0$.
$S_n = \dfrac{10}{2}(2n - 1) = 5(2n - 1)$

According to the problem, the distance in the last second equals the distance in the first $3$ seconds:
$5(2n - 1) = 45$
$2n - 1 = 9$
$2n = 10 \implies n = 5 \text{ s}$

The total time of flight is $5$ seconds. The total height of the tower is the total distance fallen in $5$ seconds:
$H = \dfrac{1}{2}gn^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (5)^2 = 5 \times 25 = 125 \text{ m}$

Answer: $125 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hockey puck is sliding due East on a frictionless ice surface. A player strikes it, applying an average force directed exactly North-West. If the puck's speed immediately after the strike is identical to its speed before the strike, what is its new direction of motion?
questions.solution:
Let the initial velocity be $\vec{v}_i = v\hat{i}$ (due East).

The average force, and therefore the change in velocity $\Delta\vec{v}$, is directed North-West. Thus, $\Delta\vec{v} = k(-\hat{i} + \hat{j})$ for some positive constant $k$.

The final velocity is given by $\vec{v}_f = \vec{v}_i + \Delta\vec{v}$.
$\vec{v}_f = v\hat{i} - k\hat{i} + k\hat{j} = (v - k)\hat{i} + k\hat{j}$.

We are given that the final speed equals the initial speed, so $|\vec{v}_f| = v$.
$(v - k)^2 + k^2 = v^2$
$v^2 - 2vk + 2k^2 = v^2$
$2k^2 - 2vk = 0$
Since $k \gt 0$, we have $k = v$.

Substituting $k = v$ back into the expression for final velocity:
$\vec{v}_f = (v - v)\hat{i} + v\hat{j} = v\hat{j}$.

The final velocity is directed along the positive y-axis, which corresponds to due North.

Answer: North

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a lift is accelerating vertically upwards, a ball dropped from its ceiling takes less time to hit the floor compared to when the lift is stationary.
Reason (R): The acceleration of the dropped ball with respect to the ground is $g$ downwards.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: When the lift is accelerating upwards with acceleration $a$, the relative acceleration of the ball with respect to the lift is $a_{\text{rel}} = g - (-a) = g + a$ (downwards). Since the effective acceleration $(g + a)$ is greater than $g$, the time taken to hit the floor $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g+a}}$ is less than the time taken in a stationary lift $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

Reason (R) is true: Once the ball is dropped, it is under free fall. Its acceleration with respect to the ground is simply the acceleration due to gravity $g$ downwards, regardless of the lift's motion.

However, the Reason does not correctly explain the Assertion. The decrease in time is due to the increased relative acceleration $(g+a)$ between the ball and the lift, not merely because the ball's acceleration with respect to the ground is $g$.

Therefore, both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The velocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph of a body projected vertically upwards from the ground is a straight line. The graph intersects the velocity axis at $20 \text{ m/s}$ and the time axis at $2 \text{ s}$. What is the ratio of the total distance covered to the magnitude of displacement of the body at $t = 3 \text{ s}$?
questions.solution:
From the given information, the velocity at $t = 0$ is $u = 20 \text{ m/s}$, and the velocity becomes zero at $t = 2 \text{ s}$.

The acceleration is the slope of the $v$-$t$ graph:
$a = \dfrac{0 - 20}{2 - 0} = -10 \text{ m/s}^2$

At $t = 3 \text{ s}$, the velocity is:
$v = u + at = 20 - 10(3) = -10 \text{ m/s}$

The displacement is the net area under the $v$-$t$ graph. The graph forms two triangles with the time axis:
Area from $t = 0$ to $t = 2 \text{ s}$ (above the axis): $A_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 20 = 20 \text{ m}$
Area from $t = 2 \text{ s}$ to $t = 3 \text{ s}$ (below the axis): $A_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times (-10) = -5 \text{ m}$

Magnitude of displacement $= |A_1 + A_2| = |20 - 5| = 15 \text{ m}$

Total distance covered $= |A_1| + |A_2| = 20 + 5 = 25 \text{ m}$

Ratio of distance to displacement $= \dfrac{25}{15} = \dfrac{5}{3}$

Answer: \dfrac{5}{3}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle starting from rest accelerates uniformly along a straight horizontal line. The ratio of the distance travelled by the particle in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second to that in the $(n+1)^{\text{th}}$ second is $5:7$. What is the value of $n$?
questions.solution:
For a particle starting from rest ($u = 0$) and moving with uniform acceleration $a$, the distance travelled in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second is given by:
$S_n = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1) = \dfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$

Similarly, the distance travelled in the $(n+1)^{\text{th}}$ second is:
$S_{n+1} = \dfrac{a}{2}[2(n+1) - 1] = \dfrac{a}{2}(2n + 1)$

According to the given condition, the ratio of these distances is $5:7$:
$\dfrac{S_n}{S_{n+1}} = \dfrac{2n - 1}{2n + 1} = \dfrac{5}{7}$

Cross-multiplying to solve for $n$:
$7(2n - 1) = 5(2n + 1)$
$14n - 7 = 10n + 5$
$4n = 12$
$n = 3$

Thus, the value of $n$ is $3$.

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bird flying horizontally due North suddenly changes its flight direction to due West, maintaining the same speed. The direction of the average acceleration of the bird during this turn is :
questions.solution:
Let the speed of the bird be $v$.

Taking East as the positive x-axis ($\hat{i}$) and North as the positive y-axis ($\hat{j}$):
Initial velocity, $\vec{v}_i = v\hat{j}$
Final velocity, $\vec{v}_f = -v\hat{i}$

The average acceleration is directed along the change in velocity ($\Delta\vec{v}$):
$\Delta\vec{v} = \vec{v}_f - \vec{v}_i = -v\hat{i} - v\hat{j}$

The vector $-v\hat{i} - v\hat{j}$ has negative x and negative y components, which corresponds to the South-West direction.
Therefore, the average acceleration is directed along South-West.

Answer: South-West

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An elevator cable snaps, causing the elevator to fall freely under gravity. At that exact instant, a person inside the elevator drops an apple from a height $h$ above the elevator floor. What is the time taken for the apple to strike the floor of the elevator?
options: It will never hit the floor
questions.solution:
When the elevator cable snaps, the elevator falls freely under gravity. Therefore, the downward acceleration of the elevator is $g$.

When the apple is dropped, it is also in free fall, so its downward acceleration is $g$.

The relative acceleration of the apple with respect to the elevator is $a_{rel} = g - g = 0$.

Since the apple is dropped from rest relative to the elevator, its initial relative velocity $u_{rel} = 0$.

Using the equation of motion $s_{rel} = u_{rel}t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{rel}t^2$, we get $s_{rel} = 0$ for any time $t$.

Since the relative displacement remains zero, the apple appears to float inside the elevator and will never hit the floor.

Answer: It will never hit the floor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car covers half the total distance of a trip at a constant speed $v_0$. The remaining half of the distance is covered in two equal time intervals with speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$. The average speed for the entire trip is:
questions.solution:
Let the total distance of the trip be $2d$.

The first half of the distance ($d$) is covered at a speed $v_0$.
Time taken for the first half, $t_1 = \dfrac{d}{v_0}$.

The second half of the distance ($d$) is covered in two equal time intervals, say $t_0$ each, with speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$.
Distance covered in this half $= v_1 t_0 + v_2 t_0 = d$
$\Rightarrow t_0 = \dfrac{d}{v_1 + v_2}$
Total time taken for the second half, $t_2 = 2t_0 = \dfrac{2d}{v_1 + v_2}$.

Total time for the entire trip, $T = t_1 + t_2 = \dfrac{d}{v_0} + \dfrac{2d}{v_1 + v_2}$
$T = d \left( \dfrac{v_1 + v_2 + 2v_0}{v_0(v_1 + v_2)} \right)$

Average speed for the entire trip, $v_{avg} = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Total time}} = \dfrac{2d}{T}$
$v_{avg} = \dfrac{2d}{d \left( \dfrac{2v_0 + v_1 + v_2}{v_0(v_1 + v_2)} \right)} = \dfrac{2v_0(v_1 + v_2)}{2v_0 + v_1 + v_2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2v_0(v_1 + v_2)}{2v_0 + v_1 + v_2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rubber ball is dropped from a height $h$ onto a hard floor. It hits the floor and bounces back perfectly elastically to the same height. Taking the downward direction as positive, which of the following correctly describes the velocity-time ($v-t$) graph for the motion of the ball from the moment it is dropped until it reaches its maximum height again?
options: Two parallel straight line segments with the same positive slope, separated by a sudden jump from a positive to a negative velocity.
A continuous V-shaped graph entirely above the time axis, starting from the origin.
A continuous zig-zag graph with alternating positive and negative slopes, starting from the origin.
A single continuous straight line starting from a negative velocity, crossing the time axis to a positive velocity.
questions.solution:
Let the downward direction be positive. The ball is dropped, so its initial velocity is zero.

During the downward fall, the acceleration is $a = +g$ (constant). The velocity increases linearly according to $v = gt$. This is represented by a straight line starting from the origin with a positive slope.

Upon perfectly elastic impact with the floor, the velocity of the ball instantly reverses its direction but maintains its magnitude. Thus, the velocity abruptly changes from a positive value ($+v_0$) to a negative value ($-v_0$). This creates a sudden jump (discontinuity) in the $v-t$ graph.

As the ball rises, it still experiences a downward acceleration of $a = +g$. The velocity changes from $-v_0$ to $0$ linearly. Since the acceleration is the same, the slope of this segment is identical to the first segment.

Therefore, the graph consists of two parallel straight line segments with a positive slope, separated by a sudden jump from positive to negative velocity.

A V-shaped graph (Option 2) incorrectly plots speed instead of velocity. A zig-zag graph (Option 3) incorrectly assumes acceleration changes direction after the bounce.

Answer: Two parallel straight line segments with the same positive slope, separated by a sudden jump from a positive to a negative velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a car travels between two cities covering the journey in two equal distance halves at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$ (where $v_1 \neq v_2$), its average speed is always less than if it had traveled at those same speeds for two equal time intervals.

Reason (R): The average speed for a journey divided into two equal distance halves is given by the arithmetic mean of the two speeds.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
For a journey divided into two equal distance halves at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$, the average speed is the harmonic mean: $v_{dist} = \dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$.

For a journey divided into two equal time intervals at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$, the average speed is the arithmetic mean: $v_{time} = \dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{2}$.

Mathematically, for any two distinct positive numbers, the harmonic mean is strictly less than the arithmetic mean ($v_{dist} \lt v_{time}$). Therefore, the Assertion (A) is true.

The Reason (R) states that the average speed for equal distance halves is the arithmetic mean, which is incorrect. It is the harmonic mean. Thus, Reason (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a ball thrown vertically upwards and returning to the ground, its acceleration is constant and directed downwards throughout the motion.
Reason (R): The speed-time graph for the entire journey of this ball is a straight line that crosses the time axis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true because a ball thrown vertically upwards moves under the influence of gravity alone (ignoring air resistance), so it experiences a constant downward acceleration ($g$) throughout its upward and downward journey.

Reason (R) is false because speed is a scalar quantity and is the magnitude of velocity. Therefore, speed can never be negative. The speed-time graph of a ball thrown upwards will decrease linearly to zero at the highest point and then increase linearly as it falls back, forming a V-shape that bounces off the time axis, rather than a straight line crossing into the negative region. A straight line crossing the time axis represents a velocity-time graph, not a speed-time graph.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The displacement-time graphs for two particles A and B are straight lines. The graph for particle A makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the displacement axis, while the graph for particle B makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the displacement axis. The ratio of the velocity of particle A to that of particle B is:
questions.solution:
The velocity of a particle is given by the slope of its displacement-time graph, which is the tangent of the angle it makes with the time axis.

Let the angles made by the graphs of A and B with the time axis be $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$ respectively.

Since the angles are given with respect to the displacement axis, we must find their complementary angles to get the angles with the time axis:
$\theta_A = 90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ$
$\theta_B = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$

The velocities are:
$v_A = \tan(30^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$
$v_B = \tan(60^\circ) = \sqrt{3}$

The ratio of their velocities is:
$\dfrac{v_A}{v_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Thus, the ratio is $1:3$.

Answer: $1:3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match the initial and final directions of a car moving at a constant speed (List-I) with the direction of the average force acting on it during the turn (List-II).

List-IList-II
(A) Moving North, turns East(I) North-West
(B) Moving East, turns South(II) North-East
(C) Moving South, turns West(III) South-West
(D) Moving West, turns North(IV) South-East

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The direction of the average force is the same as the direction of the change in velocity, $\Delta\vec{v} = \vec{v}_f - \vec{v}_i$.

Let the speed be $v$. We take East as $\hat{i}$, North as $\hat{j}$, West as $-\hat{i}$, and South as $-\hat{j}$.

(A) Moving North ($\vec{v}_i = v\hat{j}$), turns East ($\vec{v}_f = v\hat{i}$).
$\Delta\vec{v} = v\hat{i} - v\hat{j}$ (South-East). So, (A) matches (IV).

(B) Moving East ($\vec{v}_i = v\hat{i}$), turns South ($\vec{v}_f = -v\hat{j}$).
$\Delta\vec{v} = -v\hat{j} - v\hat{i}$ (South-West). So, (B) matches (III).

(C) Moving South ($\vec{v}_i = -v\hat{j}$), turns West ($\vec{v}_f = -v\hat{i}$).
$\Delta\vec{v} = -v\hat{i} - (-v\hat{j}) = -v\hat{i} + v\hat{j}$ (North-West). So, (C) matches (I).

(D) Moving West ($\vec{v}_i = -v\hat{i}$), turns North ($\vec{v}_f = v\hat{j}$).
$\Delta\vec{v} = v\hat{j} - (-v\hat{i}) = v\hat{i} + v\hat{j}$ (North-East). So, (D) matches (II).

The correct matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A drone flies parallel to a double railway track. Trains depart from stations at both ends of the track every $T$ minutes, moving at a constant speed of $80 \text{ km/h}$ in both directions. The drone meets a train moving in the opposite direction every $12 \text{ minutes}$, and overtakes a train moving in the same direction every $36 \text{ minutes}$. What is the speed of the drone and the time period $T$ of the train service?
questions.solution:
Let the speed of the drone be $v_d$ and the distance between two consecutive trains be $d$.

Since the trains depart every $T$ minutes at a speed of $v_t = 80 \text{ km/h}$, the distance between them is:
$d = v_t \times T = 80 \times \dfrac{T}{60}$ (with $T$ in minutes and $d$ in km)

For trains moving in the opposite direction, the relative speed is $v_d + 80$. The time interval between encounters is $12 \text{ min}$ ($\dfrac{1}{5} \text{ h}$).
$d = (v_d + 80) \times \dfrac{1}{5}$

For trains moving in the same direction, the drone overtakes them, so the relative speed is $v_d - 80$. The time interval is $36 \text{ min}$ ($\dfrac{3}{5} \text{ h}$).
$d = (v_d - 80) \times \dfrac{3}{5}$

Equating the two expressions for $d$:
$(v_d + 80) \times \dfrac{1}{5} = (v_d - 80) \times \dfrac{3}{5}$
$v_d + 80 = 3v_d - 240$
$2v_d = 320 \Rightarrow v_d = 160 \text{ km/h}$

Substitute $v_d$ back to find $d$:
$d = (160 + 80) \times \dfrac{1}{5} = 48 \text{ km}$

Finally, find the time period $T$:
$T = \dfrac{d}{v_t} = \dfrac{48}{80} \text{ h} = 0.6 \text{ h} = 36 \text{ min}$

Answer: $160 \text{ km/h}, 36 \text{ min}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration in a straight line. It covers the first half of its total distance with an average velocity $v_1$, and the second half of its total distance with an average velocity $v_2$. The ratio $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Let the total distance be $2d$ and the uniform acceleration be $a$.

The velocity of the particle at the start is $u = 0$.
Using the third equation of motion, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, the velocity at the midpoint (distance $d$) is $v' = \sqrt{2ad}$.
The velocity at the end of the journey (distance $2d$) is $v'' = \sqrt{2a(2d)} = 2\sqrt{ad}$.

For uniformly accelerated motion, the average velocity over any interval is the arithmetic mean of the initial and final velocities for that interval.
Average velocity for the first half, $v_1 = \dfrac{0 + \sqrt{2ad}}{2}$.
Average velocity for the second half, $v_2 = \dfrac{\sqrt{2ad} + 2\sqrt{ad}}{2}$.

The ratio is:
$\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2ad} + 2\sqrt{ad}}{\sqrt{2ad}} = 1 + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2} + 1$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2} + 1$

questions.q: A motorcyclist is travelling due East at $10\text{ m/s}$. They take a turn due North and simultaneously increase their speed to $10\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}$. The angle that the average force acting on the motorcyclist makes with the West direction is :
questions.solution:
Taking East as the positive x-axis ($\hat{i}$) and North as the positive y-axis ($\hat{j}$):
Initial velocity, $\vec{v}_i = 10\hat{i}$
Final velocity, $\vec{v}_f = 10\sqrt{3}\hat{j}$

According to Newton's second law, the average force acts in the direction of the change in velocity ($\Delta\vec{v}$):
$\Delta\vec{v} = \vec{v}_f - \vec{v}_i = -10\hat{i} + 10\sqrt{3}\hat{j}$

This vector has a negative x-component (West) and a positive y-component (North), so it lies in the North-West quadrant.
The angle $\theta$ it makes with the West direction (negative x-axis) is given by:
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{|\text{y-component}|}{|\text{x-component}|} = \dfrac{10\sqrt{3}}{10} = \sqrt{3}$

Thus, $\theta = 60^{\circ}$.
The average force is directed $60^{\circ}$ North of West.

Answer: $60^{\circ}$ North of West

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Velocity is given by $v=4 t(1-2 t)$, then find time at which velocity is maximum
questions.solution:
To find value of time at which velocity is maximum, taking differentiation of v with respect to time
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dt}}=0$
Here, $v=4 t(l-2 t)\begin{array}{lc} & \mathrm{v}=4 \mathrm{t}-8 \mathrm{t}^2 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{dt}}\left(4 \mathrm{t}-8 \mathrm{t}^2\right)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 4-16 \mathrm{t}=0 \\ \Rightarrow & \mathrm{t}=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{~s}=0.25 \mathrm{~s}\end{array}$
Again taking differentiation,
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 v}{\mathrm{dt}^2}=-16 \lt 0$
So, at $\mathrm{t}=0.25 \mathrm{~s}$ velocity is maximum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A body is projected vertically upwards. The times corresponding to height $h$ while ascending and while descending are $t_1$ and $t_2$, respectively.
Then, the velocity of projection will be (take $g$ as acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Let $v$ be initial velocity of vertical projection and $t$ be the time taken by the body to reach a height $h$ from ground.
Here, $u=u, a=-g, s=h, t=t$
Using, $s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2$, we have
$\begin{aligned}& h=u t+\frac{1}{2}(-g) t^2 \text { or } g t^2-2 u t+2 h=0 \\& \therefore t=\frac{2 u \pm \sqrt{4 u^2-4 g \times 2 h}}{2 g}=\frac{u \pm \sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g}\end{aligned}$
It means $t$ has two values, i.e.
$\begin{aligned}& t_1=\frac{u+\sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g} \\
& t_2=\frac{u-\sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g} \\& t_1+t_2=\frac{2 u}{g} \text { or } u=\frac{g\left(t_1+t_2\right)}{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is thrown upwards with a speed $u$ from a height h above the ground. The time taken by the ball to hit the ground is
questions.solution:
Time taken to reach the highest point from the height h is obtained from equation, $\mathrm{v}=\mathrm{u}-\mathrm{gt}\therefore \quad 0=\mathrm{u}-\mathrm{gt}$ or $\mathrm{t}=\frac{\mathrm{u}}{\mathrm{g}}$
Height attained above h is obtained from
$\mathrm{v}^2-\mathrm{u}^2=2(-\mathrm{g}) \mathrm{h}_1$
or $\quad 0-\mathrm{u}^2=2(-\mathrm{g}) \mathrm{h}_1$ or $\mathrm{h}_1=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2}{2 \mathrm{~g}}$
Total height, $\mathrm{h}_2=\left[\mathrm{h}_1+\mathrm{h}=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2}{2 \mathrm{~g}}+\mathrm{h}\right]$
Time taken to hit the ground is obtained from,
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{h}_2 & =\mathrm{ut}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{at}^2 \\ \frac{\mathrm{u}^2}{2 \mathrm{~g}}+\mathrm{h} & =0+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2\end{aligned}\therefore$ Total time taken, $\mathrm{t}=\sqrt{\frac{\left(\mathrm{u}^2+2 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~h}\right)}{\mathrm{g}^2}}$

questions.q: A metro train starts from rest and in 5 s achieves $108 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$. After that it moves with constant velocity and comes to rest after travelling 45 m with uniform retardation. If total distance travelled is 395 m, find total time of travelling.
questions.solution:
Given, $v=108 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}=30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
For first equation of motion
$v=u+a t\therefore \quad 30=0+a \times 5 \quad(\because u=0)$
or $\quad a=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$
So, distance travelled by metro train in 5 s
$s_1=\frac{1}{2} a t^2=\frac{1}{2} \times(6) \times(5)^2=75 \mathrm{~m}$
Distance travelled before coming to rest
$=45 \mathrm{~m}$
So, from third equation of motion
$\begin{aligned} & 0^2=(30)^2-2 a^{\prime} \times 45 \\ & \text { or } \quad a^{\prime}=\frac{30 \times 30}{2 \times 45}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 \\ & \end{aligned}$
Time taken in travelling 45 m is
$t_3=\frac{30}{10}=3 \mathrm{~s}$
Now, total distance $=395 \mathrm{~m}$
ie, $\quad 75+s^{\prime}+45=395 \mathrm{~m}$
or $s^{\prime}=395-(75+45)=275 \mathrm{~m}\therefore \quad t_2=\frac{275}{30}=9.2 \mathrm{~s}$
Hence, total time taken in whole journey
$\begin{aligned} & =t_1+t_2+t_3 \\ & =5+9.2+3 \\ & =17.2 \mathrm{~s}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A car moves from $X$ to $Y$ with a uniform speed $v_u$ and returns to $Y$ with a uniform speed $v_d$. The average speed for this round trip is
questions.solution:
Let $t_1$ and $t_2$ be times taken by the car to go from $X$ to $Y$ and then from $Y$ to $X$ respectively. Then, $t_1+t_2=\frac{X Y}{v_u}+\frac{X Y}{v_d}=X Y\left(\frac{v_u+v_d}{v_u v_d}\right)$
Total distance travelled
$=X Y+X Y=2 X Y$
Therefore, average speed of the car for this round trip is
$\begin{aligned} v_{\mathrm{av}} & =\frac{2 X Y}{X Y\left(\frac{v_u+v_d}{v_u v_d}\right)} \\ \text { or } \quad v_{\mathrm{av}} & =\frac{2 v_u v_d}{v_u+v_d}\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
A particle moves along a straight line $O X$. At a time $t$ (in second) the distance $x$ (in metre) of the particle from $O$ is given by
$x=40+12 t-t^3$
How long would the particle travel before coming to rest?
questions.solution:
Key Idea : Speed is rate of change of distance. Distance travelled by the particle is
$x=40+12 t-t^3$
We know that, speed is rate of change of distance $i e, v=\frac{d x}{d t}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad v & =\frac{d}{d t}\left(40+12 t-t^3\right) \\ & =0+12-3 t^2\end{aligned}$
but final velocity $v=0\therefore \quad 12-3 t^2=0$
or $\quad t^2=\frac{12}{3}=4$
or $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$
Hence, distance travelled by the particle before coming to rest is given by
$\begin{aligned} x & =40+12(2)-(2)^3 \\ & =40+24-8=64-8 \\ & =56 \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$

$x=a_0+\frac{a_1 t}{2}-\frac{a_2 t^2}{3}$
What is its acceleration?
questions.solution:
Key Idea : Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and velocity is the rate of change of displacement.
The displacement equation is given by
$x=a_0+\frac{a_1 t}{2}-\frac{a_2 t^2}{3}$
Velocity $=$ rate of change of displacement
ie, $\quad v=\frac{d x}{d t}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{d}{d t}\left(a_0+\frac{a_1 t}{2}-\frac{a_2 t^2}{3}\right) \\ & =0+\frac{a_1}{2}-\frac{2 a_2 t}{3} \\ & =\frac{a_1}{2}-\frac{2 a_2 t}{3}\end{aligned}$
Acceleration $=$ rate of change of velocity
$i e$, 
$\begin{aligned} a & =\frac{d v}{d t} \\ & =\frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{a_1}{2}-\frac{2 a_2}{3} t\right) \\ & =0-\frac{2 a_2}{3} \\ & =-\frac{2 a_2}{3}\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:

The value of term $A=-a \alpha e^{-\alpha t}$ decreases and of term $B=b \beta e^{\beta t}$ increases with increase in time.
As a result, velocity goes on increasing with time.
